parts.title: How accurate, consistent and easy to read are one-question and short questionnaires about physical activity? A systematic review for health monitoring
parts.abstract:
Abstract

Background

To keep track of how active people are, we need to measure their physical activity quickly and accurately. Many questionnaires about physical activity are already used in research. Even so, it is unclear which of them is the most reliable, the most valid and the easiest to use. In this systematic review, we set out to find the short questionnaires that already exist, describe and compare how well they measure activity, and judge how easy they are to read.

Methods

We followed the PRISMA statement, a widely used set of rules for carrying out and reporting systematic reviews. We searched six scientific databases for studies. We included an article if it tested the validity and/or reliability of a short questionnaire (three questions or fewer) about physical activity or exercise, meant for healthy adults. Because the studies were so different from one another, we summarized their findings in words rather than combining them with numbers. We measured how easy each questionnaire is to read using the Flesch-Kincaid formula, a standard way of scoring how hard a piece of text is to read.

Results

In total, we included 35 articles published in English or Spanish, which tested 32 different short questionnaires. The studies showed that the questionnaires had moderate to good reliability, meaning people tended to give similar answers when asked again. However, most results showed weak validity when the questionnaires were checked against measurements from devices such as movement trackers. When they were checked against other questionnaires, their validity was weak to moderate. Most of the questionnaires we assessed met our rule for being "short": people could finish them in less than one minute, either on their own or with an interviewer. However, only 17 questionnaires had a readability level showing that most people can understand them easily.

Conclusions

We found a wide variety of short questionnaires, but most of them had been tested in only one study. Short and long questionnaires turned out to be about equally valid and reliable, so we can recommend short questionnaires for use in health monitoring systems. However, the studies used very different methods to test how well the questionnaires measure activity. This makes it hard to compare the questionnaires with each other and to pick one as the best. None of the short questionnaires we assessed could tell us whether a person meets the current physical activity guidelines of the World Health Organization (WHO). When questionnaires are developed or adapted in the future, making them easy to read should be a priority, because this makes them more useful.
parts.introduction_first: Research has shown that being physically active regularly can help improve how our bodies and minds work, and can even undo some of the effects of long-lasting diseases [1]. Experts see it as key to preventing non-communicable diseases, which are illnesses that do not spread from person to person. The advice is to get 150 minutes of physical activity each week [2], eat a healthy diet, and not smoke or drink alcohol.
parts.conclusion:
Conclusion

This systematic review sheds light on how valid, reliable and easy to read short questionnaires about physical activity are. The studies used many different methods, and for some questionnaires there was not enough information about how well they measure activity. Because of this, we could not compare the questionnaires in detail or find the most accurate one. Our results show that more research on these questionnaires is needed, especially on how reliable and valid they are, how easy they are to read, and how well they work in countries where people do not speak English or in developing countries.

In recent years, health monitoring has moved away from questionnaires that people fill in themselves and towards measurements taken by devices. Part of the reason is that questionnaires have always measured activity only modestly well. Another part is that technology has improved, so movement trackers called accelerometers and other tools for measuring activity are now better and cheaper. However, measuring activity with devices has its own limits [59], and researchers have described questionnaires and devices as measuring completely different things. For now, it seems unclear what the future of health monitoring of physical activity might look like, and whether short questionnaires will still have a place in it.

In this setting, the main strength of short questionnaires is that people answer them much faster than they answer the well-known questionnaires used for health monitoring, such as the Global Physical Activity Questionnaire (GPAQ), the International Physical Activity Questionnaire (IPAQ) and the European Health Interview Survey Physical Activity Questionnaire (EHIS-PAQ). At the same time, short and long questionnaires turned out to be about equally valid and reliable. This makes short questionnaires very attractive for use in health monitoring systems. However, short questionnaires need to be improved so that they can be used to compare people with the WHO's physical activity guidelines.
parts.introduction_rest:
Even so, we need to measure physical activity accurately. Only then can we work out how much activity people need to do to stay healthy, and find out how activity is linked to other health problems and to other things people do [3]. Today, the most common way to collect information about physical activity is through questionnaires that people fill in themselves. These are often part of health monitoring systems, such as the Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System [4], the WHO STEPwise approach to noncommunicable disease risk factor surveillance [5], and the European Health Interview Survey [6]. These questionnaires have become so widely used because they are efficient. However, studies have also shown that they have limits: their answers can be biased, and the information they collect may not be fully accurate [7].

Over the years, researchers have developed many different questionnaires about physical activity. The three used most often in health monitoring around the world are the Global Physical Activity Questionnaire (GPAQ), the International Physical Activity Questionnaire (IPAQ, which also comes in a short form called IPAQ-SF), and the European Health Interview Survey Physical Activity Questionnaire (EHIS-PAQ) [8]. All three ask people about different kinds of activity, such as work, travel and free time. They ask people to describe what they did in a typical week (GPAQ and EHIS-PAQ) or in the last 7 days (IPAQ-SF). All three are fairly complex, with anywhere from seven questions (IPAQ-SF) to 16 (GPAQ).

Even so, these questionnaires measure activity only modestly well. Studies of the GPAQ [9], the IPAQ-SF [10, 11] and the EHIS-PAQ [12] have shown that they are reasonably reliable, meaning people tend to give similar answers when asked again. Their validity, however, is fairly low. A recent review of the IPAQ-SF, the GPAQ and the EHIS-PAQ found that they had low to moderate validity when checked against measurements from devices, such as movement trackers called accelerometers. When checked against other questionnaires, which also rely on people's own reports, their validity was moderate to high [8].

It is well known that questionnaires with many questions can make people feel that answering them is a heavy task [13, 14]. This has led researchers to create several short questionnaires. Unlike the detailed questionnaires described above, short questionnaires about physical activity are meant to make measuring activity simpler and quicker.

On top of this, language is currently an important topic in public health. Teaching materials for patients can help them follow their treatment, but only if they are written in a language the patient can easily understand [15]. For questionnaires about physical activity, Altschuler and colleagues [16] found clear gaps between what people understood some questions to mean and what the researchers had originally meant by them.

One feature of language is how easy it is to read, which shows how easily readers can understand the text. Research on texts used in healthcare keeps showing that materials meant for patients often need a high level of education and are too complicated for the average person [15, 17]. For questionnaires about physical activity, how easy a question is to read can affect how long a person needs to understand it. If the text is too complicated, fewer people may answer, and the answers may be less accurate.

Several earlier reviews have looked at how well questionnaires about physical activity measure activity. Van Poppel and colleagues [18] reviewed the methods used to test the validity and reliability of 85 versions of these questionnaires, and they found no clear agreement on which questionnaire is best for measuring physical activity. Helmerhost and colleagues [19] studied the reliability of 34 newly developed and 96 existing questionnaires, and also how well they matched objective measurements. Both reviews included questionnaires of any length.

As far as we know, no one has yet carried out a review focused only on how well short questionnaires about physical activity measure activity. So, at the request of people working for European health monitoring systems, we carried out this review. Our aim was to give an overview of short questionnaires about physical activity, how well they measure activity, and how easy they are to read. We wanted to find questionnaires that are short, valid, reliable and easy for the general public to understand. More broadly, we hope this review will help health monitoring systems develop further and become more alike.
parts.methods:
Methods

We carried out this review following two sets of guidelines. The first is the PRISMA statement (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses) [20], a widely used set of rules for carrying out and reporting systematic reviews. The second is the COSMIN guideline (Consensus-based Standards for the Selection of Health Measurement Instruments) [21], which gives advice on how to review questionnaires that people fill in themselves. Because we did not collect or analyse any information from participants, we did not need ethical approval or informed consent.

Where we looked for studies and how we searched

In March 2022, we searched six scientific databases: PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, CINAHL, SportDiscus and PsycInfo. We repeated the search on July 21, 2023, to find any new articles. We also checked the reference lists of earlier reviews of questionnaires about physical activity, along with other relevant publications, to find more studies. To build a thorough search, we combined keywords in two groups: one describing what was measured (physical activity) and one describing the kind of tool (a brief or short questionnaire).

The search we used was:

("physical activit*" OR "physical inactivit*")

AND

(questionnaire OR measure OR evaluat* OR assess* OR surveillance OR monitor* OR screening)

AND

("single item" OR single-item OR "single question" OR "one item" OR one-item OR "one question" OR "brief questionnaire " OR "short questionnaire " OR "brief assessment" OR "short assessment" OR "two-item*" OR "two-item*" OR "two questions" OR "brief physical activity assessment" OR "Single response" OR "Single-response")

We did not limit the search by language or by when the articles were published.

Which articles we included

We included an article in the review if it met all of these conditions:

The article described a questionnaire about physical activity or exercise that people fill in themselves, meant for healthy adults.

The questionnaire was short, with three questions or fewer.

The article tested one or more of the questionnaire's measurement properties, meaning how well it measures activity.

The article was published in a peer-reviewed journal, where other experts check the work before it is published.

We left an article out if it met any of these conditions:

The article focused on a questionnaire that measured only physical inactivity, screen time, or sedentary behavior (spending a lot of time sitting or lying down).

The questionnaire was meant only for children and teenagers, or only for people with particular health conditions.

The article did not test how well the questionnaire measures activity.

How we chose the studies

Two reviewers each checked and chose the relevant articles on their own. First, we looked at every article's title and abstract (the short summary at the start of an article). If the title or abstract showed that a study met our conditions, both reviewers read the full article to decide whether it was suitable. When needed, we also checked extra files that came with the article for more information. Whenever the two reviewers disagreed, we discussed it within the research team until we agreed.

We kept track of the articles using two computer programs: Covidence, a program for managing systematic reviews (Veritas Health Innovation, Melbourne, Australia; www.covidence.org), and EndNote X9 (Clarivate Analytics, Philadelphia, PA, USA).

What information we took from each study

One reviewer took the information from each included study and summarized it, and a second reviewer checked this work. Doing it this way reduced mistakes and bias, meaning errors or slants that could creep into the results. When the two reviewers did not agree, they discussed it until they reached the same answer.

From each study, we noted the following:

- details of the publication (the first author, the year it was published and the country);
- who took part (the number of participants, their age group and any special health conditions);
- the questionnaire or questionnaires being tested;
- who measured how active the participants were;
- which measurement properties were tested;
- any other tool used for comparison;
- how long the gap was between the two rounds of testing used to check reliability;
- the study's results.

How we judged the quality of each study

We judged the quality of each study using 18 questions from the Appraisal tool for Cross-Sectional Studies (AXIS) [22]. This tool is designed for studies that look at people at a single point in time. To judge more closely how well each questionnaire was tested for validity and reliability, we changed some of the questions. We based these changes on the COSMIN checklist for spotting bias [21] and on advice from earlier systematic reviews of tools for measuring physical activity [23].

The quality check looked at how the study was designed, how many people took part, how participants were chosen, whether the study was properly blinded (kept hidden from people who could influence the results), how experienced the people taking the measurements were, how the measurements were made, and whether the data were reported well enough. It also looked at internal consistency, meaning whether the questions in a questionnaire hang together and measure the same thing, and at six other areas (see S1 File).

Two reviewers judged each study on their own, and we settled any differences by discussing them in the research team. A study scored 1 point for each quality item it met and 0 points for each one it did not. The total score, which could range from 0 to 18, shows the risk of bias: a higher score means a better-quality study and therefore a lower risk of bias.

How we brought the findings together and compared the questionnaires

The main aim of this systematic review was to find short questionnaires that already exist and are suitable for measuring how active people are in health monitoring systems and in primary care (the first point of contact for people's health, such as a family doctor's clinic). We also wanted to compare how well these questionnaires measure activity. To do this, we summarized the relevant information from each included study separately for each questionnaire.

The included studies used a range of tests to check the reliability and validity of the questionnaires. Some studies reported results for the questionnaire's total score, while others checked reliability and validity for particular parts of the questionnaire, such as specific activities, how hard people were working, or different areas of activity. Some studies also tested these properties in smaller groups within the people who took part.

Because the studies used very different methods and did not report their results in the same standard way, we could not combine their results with numbers in a meta-analysis. Instead, we summarized the information from the studies in words, highlighting the key findings for each questionnaire. This kind of summary gives a full overview of what the studies found about reliability and validity, and shows the strengths and weaknesses of each questionnaire.

How we measured how long and how easy each questionnaire is to read

We wanted to know how quickly people could answer each questionnaire and how easy the questions are to understand. So we counted the words in each questionnaire and worked out its readability level. We calculated how long a person would be expected to take to answer it, both when filling it in alone (reading quietly) and when an interviewer reads it aloud. For this, we used each questionnaire's word count together with English reading speeds worked out by Brysbaert [24].

We calculated the readability level using the Flesch-Kincaid formula, a standard way of scoring how hard a piece of text is to read. We chose it because it is the most commonly used tool for scoring how easy written health information is to read [25]. The formula comes in two forms: the Flesch Reading-Ease-Score and the Flesch–Kincaid Grade Level. The Flesch Reading-Ease-Score gives a score from 0 to 100. A higher score means the text is easier to read, and a lower score means it is harder. The Flesch–Kincaid Grade Level matches the text to the grade level, or number of years of schooling, a person would need to understand it. We used both forms for each questionnaire, with an online calculator [26].
parts.results:
Results

How we chose the studies

Our search across six databases turned up 2,693 publications. Many of these appeared more than once, so we removed 1,394 duplicates. That left 1,299 articles, which we checked by reading their titles and short summaries (abstracts). Of these, 69 studies were good enough to read in full. Three more articles met all our rules and were added to the analysis: two that had been published recently [27, 28], and one we found by looking through the reference lists of other relevant articles [29].

We then read 34 full articles and left them out. Fifteen of them had questionnaires that were too long, and 14 were not the right kind of publication. Two did not report how people described their own physical activity and exercise, and three did not check whether their questionnaire was valid and reliable. In the end, 35 studies were included. We took information from each of them and judged how well each one was done. Fig 1 gives an overview of the search.

Fig 1

Flowchart showing how we chose the studies, following the PRISMA rules.

PA = physical activity.

What the included studies were like

S1 Table summarizes the 35 studies. Most took place in Western European countries (14 studies), the USA (11), Australia (5), Canada (2), New Zealand (2) and Japan (1). Thirty-four of the studies were published in English and one in Spanish.

Altogether, 114,199 adults were asked to complete the 32 different short questionnaires about physical activity. The number of people in each study ranged from 9 to 39,379. In 26 studies, everyone taking part was a healthy adult. Nine studies also included particular groups of people: older adults [30] [31, 32], adults who were overweight or obese [33, 34], and patients with rheumatoid arthritis [35], coronary heart disease [36, 37] or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), a long-lasting lung disease [38].

Thirty-two studies recorded who actually filled in the questionnaire. In 17 studies, people wrote the answers themselves. In the other 15, an interviewer read the questionnaire to them and recorded their answers.

The questions asked about physical activity in several ways. Six asked how much physical activity people did, and four asked how many days a week they did enough of it. Four asked how much exercise people took part in, and two asked people to compare their own activity with that of other people of the same age. The remaining 16 asked people to pick a label for their activity level, from "inactive" to "very active".

Seven studies tested the Single Item Physical Activity Measure (SIPAM) [27, 31, 39–43], five tested the Brief Physical Activity Assessment Tool (BPAAT) [38, 44–47], and two tested the Stanford Leisure-Time Activity Categorical Item (L-CAT) [33, 34]. Each of the other 29 questionnaires was tested in only one study.

How well the studies were done

We gave each study a quality score out of 18. The average score was 12, and the scores ranged from 7 to 17. Thirteen studies scored 14 or more, which can be considered high quality. Most studies described clearly what they aimed to do, how they tested the questionnaire, how they analysed the data and what they found, and their design was suitable.

However, the studies did not say much about whether the people who examined the questionnaires had enough experience with the tool. They also did not say whether these people were "blinded", meaning kept from knowing about the participants' characteristics, earlier findings or other things they had observed. Only four studies explained why they chose the number of people they studied. Many studies also did not consistently report why people dropped out or what the people who did not answer were like. S1 Table gives the quality score of each study.

How well the questionnaires measure activity

S2 Table summarizes what the studies found about reliability, validity and diagnostic accuracy. Diagnostic accuracy means how well a questionnaire can tell apart people who meet the WHO's physical activity guidelines from people who do not.

The studies used many different statistical methods to judge validity and reliability. Some looked at absolute validity, which is how closely the answers of two tools match. Others looked at relative validity, which is how well the two tools put people in the same order, from least to most active. The methods included correlations (Pearson's, Spearman's and interclass), regression, kappa statistics and the area under the receiver operating curve (AUC-ROC). A correlation measures how closely two sets of numbers rise and fall together. Regression estimates how one measurement changes as another changes. Kappa shows how much two tools agree beyond what you would expect by chance. AUC-ROC shows how well a tool separates people who meet the guidelines from people who do not.

Eleven studies tested the reliability of short questionnaires about physical activity. All of them used a test-retest method, which means asking the same people the same questions again after a while to see whether they give similar answers. The statistical methods and the time between the two rounds varied a lot from study to study. Overall, the questionnaires showed moderate to good reliability.

Thirty-four studies tested the validity of the questionnaires. To check validity, a study needs a "gold standard", a trusted reference to compare against. Thirteen studies used other questionnaires about physical activity as this reference. Fifteen compared short questionnaires with movement trackers (accelerometers) or step counters (pedometers). Twelve compared them with other objective measurements, such as body mass index (BMI) [29, 33, 48, 49], VO2 max, the most oxygen a person can use during exercise [48, 50], or doubly labeled water, a method that tracks specially marked water to measure how much energy a person burns [35].

In general, the numbers showing validity were much lower than the numbers showing reliability. Most results showed that short questionnaires had weak validity when checked against devices and other objective measurements, and weak to moderate validity when checked against other questionnaires.

How long and how easy the questionnaires are to read

S3 Table gives the full text of every questionnaire, along with how long it is and how easy it is to read. Some questionnaires were first written and used in other languages, but we measured their length and readability using the English versions.

Twenty-seven of the 32 questionnaires can be read, either quietly by the person answering or aloud by an interviewer, in less than one minute. However, some questionnaires that the studies called "brief" actually contain a lot of text and take more than a minute to read. These are the short Nordic Physical Activity Questionnaire (NPAQ), the Total Activity Measure (TAM), the Self-report Scale to Assess Habitual Physical Activity, the Stanford Leisure-Time Activity Categorical Item and the Stanford Brief Activity Survey.

We used the Flesch-Kincaid formula to work out how easy each questionnaire is to read. Only 17 of the 32 short questionnaires reached a level of "easy to read" (9) or "plain English" (8), which means most people can understand them easily. The others have long sentences, many complicated words (with three or more syllables), or both, which makes them hard to read. Seven questionnaires are fairly difficult to read. Eight were rated "difficult to read" or "very difficult to read" and need a college-level education, so people with less education will probably find them hard to understand. The original version of the SIPAM was rated "fairly difficult to read". But when it was adapted for special groups of people, with extra words added to the same sentences, it became even more complicated. For example, the version for parents was rated "very difficult to read".

Comparing the short questionnaires

Only nine of the 32 questionnaires had data on both validity and reliability, so we chose these nine for a closer comparison. Table 1 summarizes how well each one measures activity and how easy it is to read.

The Single Item Physical Activity Measure (SIPAM) asks just one question: on how many days a week do you do 30 minutes or more of physical activity, not counting housework or activity linked to your job? This questionnaire had the most studies testing its validity and reliability. It showed good reliability in every study. Its validity, however, varied a lot between studies, from poor to good, whether it was checked against devices or against other questionnaires.

Zwolinsky and colleagues (2015) also tested how well the SIPAM could tell apart people who meet the WHO's physical activity guidelines from people who do not. They compared it with the International Physical Activity Questionnaire (IPAQ), a well-known questionnaire. The SIPAM did a poor job of this compared with the IPAQ. The two questionnaires agreed only weakly when identifying people who meet the guidelines (kappa = 0.13, 95% confidence interval 0.12 to 0.14). They agreed moderately well when identifying people who are inactive (kappa = 0.45, 95% confidence interval 0.43 to 0.47) [43]. A 95% confidence interval is a range that shows how precise an estimate is: the narrower the range, the more precise the estimate.

The Brief Physical Activity Assessment Tool (BPAAT) has two questions. One asks how often and for how long a person does vigorous (hard) physical activity. The other asks how much moderate activity and walking they do in a typical week. Each question gives a score from 0 to 8, and the two scores are added together. A total of 0 to 3 means a person is not active enough, and 4 or more means they are active enough. The studies we reviewed found that the BPAAT has moderate to good reliability and validity when compared with other questionnaires. When compared with movement trackers, however, its validity was only poor to moderate.

Smith and colleagues (2005) tested a version of the BPAAT called the Three-Question Assessment, which has a separate question about moderate activity and one about walking. They found no considerable difference in validity and reliability between the two-question and three-question versions. One study also reported that more doctors preferred the two-question version, because it is shorter and therefore easier to use (Smith, 2005).

The short Nordic Physical Activity Questionnaire (NPAQ-short) has one question about moderate to vigorous activity and a second question about vigorous activity. Danquah and colleagues (2018) compared open-ended questions, where people answer in their own words, with closed-ended questions, where people pick from set answers. The open-ended version gave better results. It showed good reliability, but its validity was similar to that of other questionnaires: poor when checked against movement trackers. The analyses also showed that this questionnaire was one of the longest and was rated "difficult to read". It agreed only weakly with movement tracker data when identifying people who meet or do not meet the WHO's physical activity guidelines (kappa = 0.42).

The Total Activity Measure (TAM) has three open-ended questions about strenuous, moderate and mild activity. Its revised second version, TAM2, asks how much time a person spends at each of these levels over 7 days. When checked against movement trackers, TAM2 showed good reliability. It was long, with 241 words, and was rated "fairly difficult" to read.

The Japan Collaborative Cohort (JACC) Questionnaire has three questions. Two are about activity in free time: how much time a person spends each week on sport or physical activity (from "little" to "at least 5 hours"), and how often they do sport over the past year (from "seldom" to "at least twice a week"). The third asks how much a person walks each day (from "little" to "more than 1 hour"). After one year, the questionnaire showed moderate reliability. It also showed moderate validity when compared with a more detailed interview by a trained researcher. The questions add up to 90 words and were rated "plain English".

The Relative PA Question is the shortest of the questionnaires we compared, and it is easy to read. It asks people to compare their own activity with that of other people of the same age, and to choose from five labels, from "much more active" to "much less active". It has moderate reliability, but its validity was poor when checked against devices and other objective measurements.

The Absolute PA Question asks people to choose the description that best fits their activity level. The three choices are: (1) vigorously active for at least 30 minutes, three times a week; (2) moderately active at least three times a week; or (3) seldom active, preferring to sit and stay still. The questionnaire is fairly short. Like most of the other short questionnaires, though, it showed high reliability and poor validity when checked against devices and other objective measurements.

The Seven-Level Single-Question Scale (SR-PA L7) asks people to place themselves on a scale from "I do not move more than is necessary in my daily routines/chores" to "I participate in competitive sports and maintain my fitness through regular training". These seven levels are meant to sort people into those who keep low, medium or high activity. The scale showed poor validity when checked against movement trackers, but good reliability. It is moderately long, at 144 words, and was rated "fairly difficult to read".

The Usual PA Scale is a single question with five answer choices. It describes three activity levels: highly active, moderately active and inactive. People read the description of each level and pick the one that matches their usual activity. It was rated "plain English" and showed good reliability and validity. However, it was checked only against another questionnaire that is not well known, so more research is needed.

The Stanford Leisure-Time Activity Categorical Item (L-CAT) is a single question with six labels for activity levels, from inactive to very active. Each label has one or two sentences describing common activity patterns over the past month. These patterns differ in how often, how hard, how long and what kind of activity people do. The labels are written in "plain English", but this made the questionnaire longer than the others. The L-CAT showed high reliability, but its validity was poor when checked against step counters and movement trackers.
parts.discussion:
Discussion

In this review, we looked at how valid, reliable and easy to read short questionnaires about physical activity are for adults. As far as we know, this is the first review that focuses only on short questionnaires, and the first to check how easy they are to read. We found a large number of them (32), which shows that researchers are very interested in these tools. But it also shows that researchers have not agreed on a shared way of measuring physical activity with short questionnaires [54].

Overall, most of the questionnaires were reported to have poor or moderate validity. They were more valid when they were checked against other questionnaires that people fill in themselves than when they were checked against devices and other objective ways of measuring activity. Reliability matters a great deal, but only 11 studies tested it. About half of all the questionnaires showed moderate to good reliability. These results match other reviews of questionnaires about physical activity [18, 19, 55, 56]. Short questionnaires turned out to be about as valid and reliable as longer ones, such as the Global Physical Activity Questionnaire (GPAQ), the International Physical Activity Questionnaire (IPAQ-SF) and the European Health Interview Survey Physical Activity Questionnaire (EHIS-PAQ) [8–12].

One big difficulty in carrying out this review was that the studies did not all work in the same way. They used different methods to test the questionnaires, waited different lengths of time between repeated measurements, and used different statistical methods to analyse their data. Complete information on validity and reliability was available for only nine questionnaires, so only those could be compared in more detail. Even so, we could not find any single questionnaire that is the most accurate.

The Single Item Physical Activity Measure (SIPAM) had the most studies on its validity and reliability. However, its validity varied a lot, from poor to good. On top of that, it is hard to read. The Usual Physical Activity Scale is another example. It has good validity and reliability, but it was studied in only one study, and that study did not check it against measurements from devices.

In general, the quality of the studies we included was modest. The most common weaknesses were fairly small groups of people, no explanation of why a group was that size, and a poor description of how validity and reliability were tested. Most studies also used convenience samples, meaning they asked people who were easy to reach, such as people in their own area. Because of this, we cannot tell whether the questionnaires would measure activity differently in adults with different levels of income, social standing or education.

The questionnaires also measured physical activity in different ways, which made it even harder to compare them directly. For example, the SIPAM asks how many days a week a person does 30 minutes or more of physical activity. The Absolute Physical Activity Questionnaire asks people to choose from several descriptions of different activity levels. The Relative Physical Activity question asks people to compare their own activity with that of other people. Some questionnaires, such as the Total Activity Measure (TAM), try to measure the total amount of moderate-to-vigorous physical activity. Others focus on particular kinds of activity, and still others measure only physical activity during free time.

This variety can partly be explained by the effort to keep questionnaires short, which means leaving out some parts of physical activity: its type, how long it lasts, how hard it is, and the total amount. But it could also mean that researchers do not share a common view of which parts of physical activity short questionnaires should measure. We should also keep in mind that none of the short questionnaires we reviewed could tell us whether a person meets the WHO's physical activity guidelines [2]. This raises an important question: should specialists work together to improve today's short questionnaires so that they meet the needs of health monitoring systems?

All of the studies we included took place in highly developed countries, and 24 of them took place in English-speaking countries. This most certainly biased our results, because words for physical activity differ from language to language, and so does how well people can read and understand written text [57]. In the end, many more studies on the reliability and validity of these questionnaires are needed in developing countries, so that we can judge more accurately whether they are suitable for health monitoring systems around the world. To encourage this kind of research, research teams from these countries need to be given chances to win funding.

Our results show that many of the questionnaires are hard to read. This is especially worrying, because most of them were tested in developed countries where people can generally read quite well. Poor readability may be linked to the modest quality of measurement that these questionnaires usually have. This shows that today's questionnaires need to be revised with their readability and language in mind. It is also crucial to keep this in mind when new questionnaires are developed. Questionnaires that are easier to read, or that were even developed together with the groups of people they are meant for [58], are likely to measure activity better. This would also make a stronger case for including them in health monitoring systems. For now, however, there is very little research linking short questionnaires and how well they measure activity to how easy they are to read. Learning more in this area would also help longer questionnaires, such as the IPAQ and the GPAQ, which are widely used in health monitoring and may also be hard to read.

Our review has some limitations. We searched only scientific databases and included only studies published in scientific journals that other experts had checked before publication. This can lead to publication bias, because we left out all other kinds of publications and "gray literature", such as reports from governments or organizations that are not published in journals. The studies used different methods and conditions, which made it hard to compare their findings. It also meant we could only describe the differences between the tools in words, rather than analyse the data with numbers. This made our results more subjective and made it harder to find the tools that measure activity best. We should also keep in mind that the Flesch-Kincaid formula was designed for longer texts and was not adapted for short questionnaires. So the readability levels of the questionnaires we present here should be read with caution.

Recommendations for health monitoring of physical activity:

Based on the results of this systematic review, we recommend that experts and decision-makers keep the following points in mind when they develop health monitoring systems further or make them more alike:

Shorter questionnaires could be used instead of long ones in some situations, because they show similar validity and reliability. Their main advantage is that people spend less time answering them, which matters both for health monitoring systems and for primary care, the everyday care people get from their local doctor. Still, we should remember that short questionnaires can collect only a fairly small amount of information, so they are not suitable for every purpose of measuring physical activity.

Most questionnaires aim to find people who are not active enough. However, none of the questionnaires we reviewed covers all the parts of the WHO's full physical activity guidelines: both how long people should do moderate and vigorous physical activity, and how often they should do strength training each week. This shows that we need to discuss what questionnaires should include, and that new tools could be developed based on the WHO guidelines.

When questionnaires are developed, tested and translated, their language needs to be considered. Possible ways to make questionnaires easier to read and understand include working with linguists, who are experts in language, and involving different groups of people in the development process.
